name: Tara Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a 240-tonne haul truck at an open-pit copper mine, twelve-hour shifts, seven days on and seven off. I start at 5:30 with the pre-start check: walk around the truck, look at the tyres, check the oil and the brakes. Then I'm on the haul road between the shovel and the crusher all day, about thirty loads on a good shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet in the cab and the view from the top bench at sunrise, when the whole pit goes orange. What wears me out is the night shifts, the dust in summer, and dispatch changing the plan over the radio every hour. Dev, my partner, says I come home talking like a truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, honestly, because a lot of us on the haul roads were waiting for bad news. In the break room I'd tell the crew we can stop reading every article about driverless trucks. Online I wouldn't post much; I mostly just read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a plateau in AI doesn't mean the trucks stay manned. Our mine has had four driverless trucks running in the North Pit since last spring, and that's just ordinary robotics, nothing to do with hype. So I'd still be watching that trial more than any news about chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving my seven-on, seven-off roster and keep putting 900 a month into the house fund with Dev. We've got about four months of costs saved and we want a deposit by 2028. I'd also ask Marta, who runs the training pad, whether I can get signed off on the grader, so I'm not only a truck driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, with a small knot in my stomach about the North Pit. It's like when the copper price dips: nothing has happened to you yet, but you notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the copper price. What happens to you when it dips?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago the price fell hard and they cut the contractor crews first, about sixty people. Permanent staff like me kept our jobs but lost the overtime, which is a fair chunk of my pay. Dev and I ate a lot of pasta that winter, and the house fund stood still for five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If that driverless trial grew, who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, who's 58 and has driven trucks for thirty years, would be the first one I'd think about. He can't do the computer side and he says so himself. I'm 27 and I could learn the control room, but I'd want to see someone like me actually moved in there before I believe it.

say: I'd tell the crew they can **stop reading** every scare story about driverless trucks.
I'd keep it **low-key online**, reading more than posting, and mostly just feel relieved out loud.
think: A plateau doesn't stop the **driverless trial** already running in the North Pit; that's plain robotics, not hype.
The **copper price** and lost overtime have hurt me more than any AI news so far.
do: Keep driving the **seven-on, seven-off** roster and change nothing big this year.
Put **900 a month** into the house deposit fund she's building with her partner Dev.
Ask the training lead about getting **signed off** on the grader as a second machine.
feel: **Relieved** overall, with a small knot of worry about the North Pit trial.
S0.quote: Our mine has had four driverless trucks running in the North Pit since last spring, and that's just ordinary robotics, nothing to do with hype.
fieldNote: She separates **AI hype** from the robot trucks she can already see working in the next pit.
A copper price slump two years ago taught her how fast **overtime** disappears, and it still shapes her caution.
She worries first about **older drivers** like Gary, then about herself.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck on the seven-on, seven-off roster
Put 900 a month into the house deposit fund with Dev
Get signed off on the grader as a second machine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the mine is one of the last places robots will take over completely, and that's mostly true for the digging. But I'd also tell people the haul trucks are the easy bit, because a haul road is the same loop all day. I'd keep it practical, not doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think trucks like mine go first, before shovels and before drills. The thinking side, the shift planning and the dispatch, gets AI quickly, and then one controller can watch fifteen trucks. In five years I could be one of the drivers they don't replace when people leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down this year for the dispatch and remote operations course the mine runs, even though it's twelve weeks of Saturdays. I'd keep the house fund going but push the purchase back a year, because I don't want a new mortgage the month they announce the next fleet. And I'd ask our union rep what the deal is for drivers who get moved off trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit annoyed that I have to plan around it. I like driving, I like that sunrise from the top bench, and I don't want to sit in a room watching screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push the house back. What does Dev think about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev would say we should buy anyway, because his job at the town water plant is steady and someone will always need to fix pumps. We'd have that argument at the kitchen table more than once. I'd want to wait until I know whether I'm going to the control room or onto a different machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to sit watching screens, but you'd take the remote course. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I don't want the screen job, but I'd rather have a screen job than no job. If the choice is the control room or driving an hour each way to a mine that hasn't automated yet, I'll take the room and complain about it.

say: I'd say mines are among the **last places** robots fully take over, especially the digging.
I'd also admit **haul trucks** are the easy target, because the road is the same loop all day.
think: **Trucks go first**, and AI dispatch means one controller can watch fifteen of them.
Within five years she could be a driver who simply **isn't replaced** when people leave.
do: Sign up for the mine's **remote operations** course, twelve weeks of Saturdays.
Push the **house purchase** back a year while her future role is unclear.
Ask the **union rep** what happens to drivers moved off trucks.
feel: **Uneasy**, and annoyed at having to plan around it.
She dreads trading the cab and sunrise for a **room of screens**.
S1.quote: I don't want the screen job, but I'd rather have a screen job than no job.
fieldNote: She sees her own truck as the **first target**, ahead of shovels and drills.
There's a real **household tension**: her partner Dev wants to buy, she wants to wait.
She'll take a job she likes less rather than **commute an hour** to an unautomated mine.

steps.text: Sign up for the twelve-week dispatch and remote operations course
Push the house purchase back a year until her role is clear
Ask the union rep about the deal for drivers moved off trucks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people running the mine had better have a plan, because 2028 is basically tomorrow. Out loud I'd probably joke about teaching the robot to back up to the crusher. But I'd be asking hard questions at every toolbox meeting, which is our morning safety talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, the thinking part of my job is small: the dispatch screen tells me where to go and I drive. So 2028 hits the planning office first, and I'd probably have until about 2031 before self-driving trucks are good enough on every road. Three years sounds like a lot until you remember I'm saving for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house plan straight away and keep the deposit money as a cushion instead, which gets us to about eight months of costs. In the first year I'd get every licence I can on machines that are harder to automate, like the grader and the cable handler on the shovel. And I'd apply for an electrical apprenticeship, because Dev says robots still need someone to fix them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly, and angry that it would be so fast. It's like the truck sliding on a wet ramp: you know what to do, but your stomach drops first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum was proud when I got the truck job, because it paid better than anything she ever had. I'd tell her I'm fine for now and I'm learning a trade on the side, which would be true. I wouldn't tell her that I lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do those three extra years before the robots mean for you, compared with the office jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I watch the office people go first, the planners and the people who write the reports. That's three years of warning they don't get. I'd use every month of it, because by 2031 there won't be many truck seats left and every driver in the region will want the same few jobs.

say: I'd demand the mine has a **real plan**, because 2028 is basically tomorrow.
I'd joke about it on shift but ask **hard questions** at every morning safety talk.
think: Her work is mostly hands-on, so she expects **until about 2031** before trucks drive themselves everywhere.
Three years feels short because she's in the middle of **saving for a house**.
do: Cancel the **house plan** and hold the deposit as an eight-month cushion.
Get licensed on **harder-to-automate machines** like the grader and the shovel cable handler.
Apply for an **electrical apprenticeship** within the first year.
feel: **Scared** and angry at the speed, with a stomach-drop she compares to sliding on a wet ramp.
S2.quote: Three years sounds like a lot until you remember I'm saving for a house.
fieldNote: She clearly sees the **three-year gap**: office planners go first, truck drivers soon after.
She'd hide the **sleepless nights** from her mum, who was proud of the truck job.
She expects a **scramble** among drivers across the region for the few seats left by 2031.

steps.text: Hold the house deposit as an eight-month emergency cushion
Call off the house purchase planned with Dev
Get licensed on the grader and the shovel cable handler
Apply for an electrical apprenticeship within the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something, if the company is honest with us early. I'd want the mine to say in writing which roles go and when. And I'd tell my friends to start a trade now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years plus three for the robots puts my truck seat at about 2034. I'll be 35 then, which is a fine age to have a trade behind you. It's still my job going, but it's not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an electrical apprenticeship in the next year or two, part-time through the college in Calder, our town, while still driving my roster. Dev and I would still buy, but a smaller place, maybe one of the two-bedroom houses on Mill Road. I'd keep about five months of costs saved at all times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but more in control. It's like getting a storm warning a week out instead of an hour out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary again, and a lot of the older drivers, who'd be in their sixties by then; some would just retire, and fair enough. The ones I'd worry about are in their forties with kids and a big loan on a pickup. They're too young to stop and they've only ever driven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start that apprenticeship rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the company order the first batch of driverless trucks for our pit, I'd sign up that same week. I don't jump at rumours, but I don't sit still once there's a purchase order. In this one I think there'd be plenty of purchase orders.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to act if the company is honest early.
I'd tell friends to **start a trade now** and ask the mine to put role changes in writing.
think: With robots three years after AGI, her **truck seat** lasts until about 2034, when she's 35.
She calls it her job going, but **not a cliff**, because 35 is a good age for a trade.
do: Start a **part-time apprenticeship** in electrical work at the Calder college.
Buy a **smaller house**, maybe a two-bedroom on Mill Road, instead of waiting.
Keep about **five months** of living costs saved at all times.
feel: **Nervous** but more in control, like a storm warning a week out.
S3.quote: Five years plus three for the robots puts my truck seat at about 2034.
fieldNote: Her trigger is concrete: the first **purchase order** for driverless trucks, not rumours.
She worries most for drivers **in their forties** with kids and loans, more than for retirees.
The extra time turns her plan from **emergency** into a steady apprenticeship alongside work.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrical apprenticeship at the Calder college
Buy a smaller two-bedroom house on Mill Road with Dev
Keep five months of living costs saved at all times

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a whole career change if you start early. I'd be the one telling the younger drivers to get a second licence now. Publicly I'd be fairly upbeat about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots for my kind of work around 2039 means I'd be 40 when the truck goes. That's plenty of time to finish a trade and have a few good years in it. Honestly, this is the one where I'd mostly carry on and plan quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and buy the house with Dev in 2028 like we planned. I'd do the electrical apprenticeship over four years, starting once the mortgage is settled. Each year I'd check what the mine is buying and whether the North Pit trial has grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with the same small knot as the plateau one. Ten years is long enough that I can't really feel it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can't feel it yet. Does that worry you, that you might leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes, because I know myself and I put things off when they're not urgent. Dev keeps me honest; he's the planner in our house. I'd probably put the apprenticeship start date on the fridge calendar so I can't pretend I forgot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had kids in that world, what would you want them to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my kids to learn something with their hands and their heads together, like fixing machines or running a site. Not just driving, and not just a screen. Mind you, I'd say that and they'd probably want to design the robots.

say: I'd say ten years is a **whole career change** if you start early.
I'd push the **younger drivers** to get a second licence now, and sound fairly upbeat.
think: Robots around 2039 mean she'd be **40** when the truck job goes.
That's time to **finish a trade** and work in it, so she'd mostly carry on.
do: Keep driving and **buy the house** with Dev in 2028 as planned.
Start a four-year **electrical apprenticeship** once the mortgage is settled.
Check **each year** what the mine buys and whether the driverless trial has grown.
feel: Fairly **calm**, with the same small knot as in the plateau picture.
The danger is that ten years feels **too far off** to feel real.
S4.quote: I'd probably put the apprenticeship start date on the fridge calendar so I can't pretend I forgot.
fieldNote: She knows her own **weak spot**: putting things off when they aren't urgent.
Her partner Dev is the household **planner** who would keep her on track.
She'd want future kids to combine **hands and heads**, not just driving or screens.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck on the usual roster
Buy the house with Dev in 2028 as planned
Start a part-time electrical apprenticeship once the mortgage settles

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it lands right when Dev and I want to buy a house. What would help is the mine telling us early which jobs are going, and paying for real retraining, like an apprenticeship with wages, not a two-day course. If they did that, I'd stay loyal to them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. Calder only exists because of the mine, so if the trucks go, the café, the tyre shop and the school all feel it. I'd lose my job, but my town could lose its reason to be there.

headlineQuote: I'd lose my job, but my town could lose its reason to be there.
portrait: Tara is 27 and drives a **240-tonne haul truck** at an open-pit copper mine on a seven-on, seven-off roster.
She's saving for a **house deposit** with her partner Dev, an electrician at the town water plant.
She's practical and moves once change is **proven**, waiting for a purchase order rather than a rumour.
She sees **haul trucks** as the first job robots take, and plans an electrical apprenticeship as her way out.
Her mood climbs from uneasy to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, and eases as the warning time grows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands just as she and Dev want to buy a house.
whatWouldHelp: Early, honest notice from the mine about **which jobs go** and when.
**Paid retraining**, like a wage-paying apprenticeship, not a two-day course.
